title: 2026 Bespoked Dresden Picks 03: Alonukis, Alutech, Cyber, Meerglas, Must, Sentient, Starfish, Vapour – John Watson
content:
Guten morgen! We’re back in Saxony at the Flughafen Dresden for the 2026 Bespoked Dresden showcase. Paul and John spent the weekend at the world’s largest framebuilder showcase, selecting bikes to document for The Radavist’s coverage of the event. Check out our picks 03 from Alonukis, Alutech, Cyber, Meerglas, Must, Sentient, Starfish, and Vapour below!

The Radavist thanks Brooks England for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Dresden coverage and our independent Reportage!

Alonukis x Too Tired Gatherer Rigid 29er – John Watson

Johannes Wandinger’s Alonukis Frameworks is based in Murnau am Staffelsee, Germany, in the Bavarian Alps region. For this year’s 2026 Bespoked Dresden show, Johannes brought this stunning truss fork 29er he built for longtime collaborator Sebastian Strobl of Too Tired Cycles in Regensburg, Germany.

The eye-catcher of this build is the stunning celeste green truss fork, which features couples Johannes made himself. It, along with the matching stem, is finished in a structured powder coat, inspired by the construction trucks and tradie vehicles found in his region of the Bavarian Alps.

As an example of the global connectivity found within makers, Johannes found inspiration in Cjell Mone’s signature single-speed tensioner design. The way you achieve your desired tension is to loosen each bolt on the drive and non-drive side, pull the dropout forward, center the wheel, and then tighten the bolts again. Thanks to knurling on the sleeved chainstay, there is enough purchase to ensure the dropouts stay in the desired location. The frame was designed to clear a 29 x 2.6″ tire with room to spare.

The bike features a Too Tired Flipside chainring and utilizes a spider adaptor for the vintage cranks. The Flipside is designed to fit 5-arm cranksets with a 94 mm or 110 mm bolt circle diameter and comes in a champagne finish. Each ring is machined from 7075-T6 aluminum in Europe and works with all 7 to 12-speed chains.

Rigid single-speeds are inherently simplistic by design, but the combination of truss fork, tensioning, and the beeswax finish on the frame elevates this stunning steed to a show-stopping level. As the crowds entered the venue Saturday morning, Johannes was fielding many attentive eyes and questions. Another favorite detail is the Alpine Edelweiss flower head badge, which a jeweler friend made for him in silver.

Stunning bike, Johannes. Well done.

@AlunukisFrameworks @TooTiredCycles

Alutech Cycles Punk 32er Prototype – John Watson

Like many domestic companies in Germany, it was the COVID-19 pandemic that drove Alutech’s founder Jürgen Schlender to return frame production to Ascheffel, Germany. Known for its trail bikes, the brand displayed a rolling prototype at the 2026 Bespoked Dresden show called the Punk A1.0.

Both the 32er aluminum frame and the dual crown fork are working prototypes. Jürgen specifically made the fork for Bespoked. What’s unique about it is that the handlebars are split down the middle and clamped to the top of the stanchions. This then allows for stealth cable routing into the fork and frame.

Jürgen says the bike could possibly go into production, depending on demand, so if you’re interested, be sure to holler at Alutech. Many thanks to his daughter for standing in for him.

@AlutechCycles

Cyber Cycles Grawall 32er – John Watson

Krawallbruder means a brawler, or someone who wants to get rowdy. This word kept swishing around in Cyber Cycles’ owner Christian Thomas’ mind when it came to designing a 32er for the 2026 Bespoked Dresden show. Combining Krawall and gravel, he landed on the Grawall name. Cyber Cycles’ design office is based in Jena, Germany, with frame and parts production under Stefano Agresti’s control, based in Offenbach/Main, Germany.

Like all projects from Cyber Cycles, this Grawall is full of nice, carefully designed, and masterfully executed details. The new prototype Vector fork was designed to be built for various wheel sizes and offsets from titanium. Taking advantage of the SON hub’s Self-Connecting System SL for ease of dynamo deployment.

Also made from titanium is the prototype Cyber Cycles stem, which features a Paul Component Engineering faceplate as well as internal routing. Back on the rear end of the bike, Christian designed a Syntace-inspired hooded UDH dropout with eccentric hardware. He hopes to sell these to builders in the coming months.

It’s always a pleasure to see what Christian brings to Bespoked each year. I really love his cranks, and it’s exciting to see future products being developed.

@CyberCycles

Meerglas Dirt Rando – John Watson

Thomas Becker’s Meerglas-Fahrräder is renowned worldwide for its pristine randonneuring bikes. Inside a humble shop located in Groß Lüben in the Prignitz region of Brandenburg, Germany, Tom sculpts stunning bikes using traditional methods. Some might treat these one-of-one beauties as precious objects, but Tom’s not one of those people.

For him, a bike is a bike and it ought to be ridden. Eagle-eyed readers of The Radavist might recognize this bike from our 2024 Bespoked Dresden coverage over here on The Radavist, where the bike was displayed with a complete balleur parts setup from Black Forest-based Tune. Since then, it’s gotten considerably dirtier and is covered in beausage, or beauty through usage, marks.

Noting the part spec swap, Tom commented, “You don’t need these fancy hubs; just Shimano Zora and Dia Compe is fine! But I do love the Tune saddle, so I kept that on the bike…” he continued. Having ridden to Dresden from his home shop, his bike was by far the heaviest I documented at the show, with a hardware store spec ratchet strap holding his front luggage to the rack.

“Who cares about weight? It does not matter,” he smiled at me, laughing about the absurd lengths people go to achieve an über-light randonneuring setup. Tom’s work has been acclaimed by fabled legend Peter Weigle and his Connecticut-based French Fender Day. Over in Germany, Tom throws Fenderfest, a European sibling to French Fender Day, and for Tom, riding bikes, camping, and partying with friends is where the joys of life are found. That, and the talisman his daughter made him, which he brings on every ride.

“For me, I need to find a balance between work and life. I want to be around more for my family,” he said, to which I replied, “Bikes will always be there…” Tom, it was a delight catching up with you. Thank you for your time, and ride safe, friend.

@MeerglasFrameworks

Must Otivao Capra Adventure Mini-Velo – Paul Kalifatidi

When John and I showed up on Thursday morning to check out the venue and see any of the bikes that had already been put out for display, I immediately spotted this fantastic folding contraption from Must. The Otivao Adventure Bike folds up and attaches to an including backpack: hike up, ride down. It doesn’t even have pedals or a drivetrain. If there had been a “Best Strider” award, this surely would have won.

Johannes Müller made the original prototype, a hardtail version, for a customer who had knee issues. Hiking up a mountain was not difficult, but going down was. The solution was this bike. It makes descending a hiking trail faster, easier, and changes the experience. Johannes told me that you can’t really ride it like a downhill bike due to its small wheels, but it is still quite fun. Again, it is more of a hiking solution than a dedicated riding bike, and I think that is perfectly ok. Frankly, I think its amazing. Where I live, we have lots of multi-use trails where this bike would be quite fun.

It folds up quite easily, I was able to do it without any guidance and in about 30 seconds, minus wheel removal and backpack install. The headtube is on a hinge and the lower shock mount is a removable pin, allowing the rear triangle to fold into the bike and the fork to lay against the downtube. The footpegs, which Johannes machines in his workshop, fold up as well. Not that I’m always looking to inject Wisconsin into a story, but I found it just a smidge comical that I flew all the way to Europe to find footpegs that were modeled after a Harley-Davidson motorcycle part.

This bike will likely never exist with a drivetrain, for multiple reasons. The rear pivot is in the wrong place, and an idler pulley would simply add too much weight and complexity. There’s no point in deviating from the main goal: hike up and have fun on the way down. Thank you, Johannes, for being my welcoming party to the fantastic and highly experimental European bike scene.

@MustCycle

Sentient Works Griffyn Full Suspension Cargo Bike – John Watson

Tullen Dawson of Sentient Works had a rough go getting to the 2026 Bespoked Dresden show. First, it was the canceled flight; then it was a hassle-filled bus ride at midnight, and come the morning of the show, he hadn’t slept much. Dragging him down to my photo spot, I was excited to see my friend from Wales and hear all about the latest version of the Griffyn, a bike I documented at the 2026 Bespoked UK show.

“We’ve sold ten frames…” he said, acting surprised. “And they’re going all over the world. There’s an order in Canada, even!” Tullen’s eyes were brightening up. This frame is the current edition, with some minor updates and tweaks. Namely, this is the longer wheelbase version, bringing in a longer front overall configuration for bigger riders.

Once he started building this for the show, he realized he didn’t have enough tubing. “I fucked up and ran out of top tubes,” he said, “So I had to use a seat tube, which is larger in diameter; then the linkage didn’t clear, so I had to notch it.” At this point, he began to chuckle as I peered in with my camera. “Prototypes!” I laughed. “And yeah, don’t forget to shoot the Exposure light!” he said, chuckling. We had shot the bike previously, and he had forgotten the light.

The linkage is fully CNC-milled, and the rear wheel travel is now at a 1:2.1 leverage ratio with a 60 mm stroke, with the front still coming in at 120 mm travel. Also new on the bike are the prototype Sentient bullmoose bars, yet to be named. Manitou has been working with Sentient on a more engineering-approved steering bar attachment method. This new device replaces the crown race and offers a more secure connection, whereas the old design clamped to the stanchion itself.

There were two Griffyn bikes displayed. The other belonged to John from Manitou, who handles OE sales to manufacturers. John’s bike was dirty and had been ridden extensively. Surprisingly, this was his first full-suspension bike. And it’s a cargo bike!

Where will the Griffyn model go next? Tullen is unsure. He wants to complete this batch and work on the next project. Sentient Works is an incubator for ideas, not a full-blown production house. Tullen did mention that he’d like to do a hardtail design in the future. So perhaps we’ll see that at the 2027 Bespoked UK showcase.

Mate, it’s always a pleasure to see you. Thanks for everything.

@SentientWorks

Starfish Bicycles Randonneur – John Watson

Tore Juncher Jørgensen’s Starfish Bicycles is based in Sydfyn (South Funen), Denmark. For the 2026 Bespoked Dresden show, they brought this brightly colored randonneuring bike, which won Best in Show. It’s hard to beat these frame proportions for a drop-bar bike, which oozes style and practicality.

“Soft bikes for soft people” is engraved on the headtube badge and “prototype” on the seat tube. Tore wanted to build a larger size of the Starfish production bike for a customer named Mikkel. The dropouts are waterjet-cut from stainless steel, featuring a heart. There’s internal dynamo routing, and the bike features low trail, around 43 mm, with a 65 mm fork rake.

The cutout heart theme continues to the chainring guard, making the bike more pant-friendly for the owner, who will also be using it to commute. With subtle details and a no-nonsense approach to design and fabrication, it’s amazing that this bike won best in show. Oftentimes, super experimental bikes that might not be the most practical get roped into that banner, so it’s refreshing to see such a beautifully-executed design get some exposure, too.

Tore requested a portrait shot through the frame, similar to what Paul’s been doing with his showcase coverage. It was great chatting with you, Tore! Well done and well deserved!

@StarfishCycles

Vapour Cycles Batmobike – Paul Kalifatidi

We’ll finish this round-up with something wildly different from our usual choices: a highly experimental and highly carbon fiber road bike that would look more fitting on the set of the next Batman movie than anywhere else. I intentionally photoshopped out the edges of the above image, where you would see the railings of the tunnel in which I was shooting, as the lighting and tile reminded me of the giant underground laboratory from The Dark Knight (2008). And no, Val, the creator of this beast, did not have a batman costume. Yes, I’m sad too.

This bike is more of a concept than anything else, Val wanted to put his production and design capabilities to the test. I’d say he succeeded. The bike was assembled using a variety of carbon fiber components, and it is actually somewhat of a lugged construction. The joints of the bike were made using 3d printed molds to create the carbon fiber structures while the main tubes are filament wound using a machine of Val’s own design. If you check out his Instagram, linked below, you’ll see just how experimental he get in his secret Berlin workshop.

I asked Val if he had put it in a wind tunnel, and he told me that he had only finished it a few days before the show. Using Computational Fluid Dynamics software, he did find out that not having a seattube was actually less aero. But, screw that, it looks crazy without a seatpost. When pushing quite firm on the saddle, I could feel the frame flex a tad, and I’m curious if it actually rides comfortably. It’s inspired by the iconic soft-ride bikes, afterall.

I hope that you start to see just how wild and experimental the bikes were at Bespoked. John has told me that he respects the experimental and self-reliant nature of the European framebuilding scene, and I immediately noticed that when walking around the venue on day one. Val, thanks for pushing it to the limit.

@VapourCycles

We’ve got a lot more on the way, so stay tuned. Which bike could you see yourself riding? Let us know in the comments!
